---
title: D3.js
---

[D3.js](https://d3js.org/) can turn a scientific model into a visual explanation
that learners can manipulate directly. In Quarto, D3 works particularly well when
several parts of a figure should respond to the same input, or when the marks in a
figure need custom appearance, movement, or interaction.

The example below is intentionally modest. It uses radioactive decay as plausible
course content, but its main purpose is to show a reusable authoring pattern:

- an Observable input controls the state of the explanation;
- one small data model drives two coordinated views;
- D3 binds that data to SVG elements and updates them in place; and
- a transition helps learners see what changed.

## A coordinated interactive figure

Move the slider through five half-lives. The grid shows the state of 100 individual
nuclei, while the chart shows the same realization as an aggregate count. Select
**Generate another sample** to see a different stochastic realization without
changing the theoretical curve.

<style>
.d3-decay-demo {

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
d3 = require("d3@7")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof time = Inputs.range([0, 5], {
  value: 0,
  step: 0.1,
  label: "Time (half-lives)"
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof sample = Inputs.button("Generate another sample", {
  value: 0,
  reduce: value => value + 1
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
function seededRandom(seed) {
  let state = seed >>> 0;
  return () => {
    state = (1664525 * state + 1013904223) >>> 0;
    return state / 4294967296;
  };
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
nuclei = {
  const random = seededRandom(2027 + sample * 7919);
  return d3.range(100).map(id => ({
    id,
    row: Math.floor(id / 10),
    column: id % 10,
    decayTime: -Math.log2(1 - random())
  }));
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
observed = d3.range(0, 5.001, 0.05).map(t => ({
  time: t,
  remaining: nuclei.filter(d => d.decayTime > t).length
}))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
chartState = {
  const width = 900;
  const height = 420;
  const grid = {x: 42, y: 92, spacing: 27};
  const plot = {left: 405, right: 868, top: 78, bottom: 350};
  const x = d3.scaleLinear([0, 5], [plot.left, plot.right]);
  const y = d3.scaleLinear([0, 100], [plot.bottom, plot.top]);
  const reducedMotion = matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches;

  const svg = d3.create("svg")
    .attr("viewBox", [0, 0, width, height])
    .attr("role", "img")
    .attr("aria-labelledby", "decay-title decay-description")
    .style("display", "block")
    .style("width", "100%")
    .style("height", "auto")
    .style("max-width", "900px")
    .style("font-family", "var(--bs-body-font-family, sans-serif)");

  svg.append("title")
    .attr("id", "decay-title")
    .text("Interactive radioactive decay realization");
  const description = svg.append("desc").attr("id", "decay-description");

  svg.append("rect")
    .attr("x", 1).attr("y", 1)
    .attr("width", width - 2).attr("height", height - 2)
    .attr("rx", 8)
    .attr("fill", "var(--bs-body-bg, white)")
    .attr("stroke", "var(--bs-border-color, #ced4da)");

  svg.append("text")
    .attr("x", grid.x).attr("y", 46)
    .attr("font-size", 17).attr("font-weight", 650)
    .attr("fill", "currentColor").text("Individual nuclei");

  const countLabel = svg.append("text")
    .attr("x", grid.x).attr("y", 70)
    .attr("font-size", 14).attr("fill", "currentColor");

  const circles = svg.append("g")
    .attr("aria-hidden", "true")
    .selectAll("circle")
    .data(nuclei, d => d.id)
    .join("circle")
    .attr("cx", d => grid.x + d.column * grid.spacing)
    .attr("cy", d => grid.y + d.row * grid.spacing)
    .attr("r", 9).attr("stroke-width", 2);

  svg.append("text")
    .attr("x", plot.left).attr("y", 46)
    .attr("font-size", 17).attr("font-weight", 650)
    .attr("fill", "currentColor").text("The same sample, summarized");

  svg.append("g")
    .attr("transform", `translate(0,${plot.bottom})`)
    .call(d3.axisBottom(x).ticks(5))
    .call(g => g.selectAll("path,line").attr("stroke", "currentColor"))
    .call(g => g.selectAll("text").attr("fill", "currentColor"));

  svg.append("g")
    .attr("transform", `translate(${plot.left},0)`)
    .call(d3.axisLeft(y).ticks(5))
    .call(g => g.selectAll("path,line").attr("stroke", "currentColor"))
    .call(g => g.selectAll("text").attr("fill", "currentColor"));

  svg.append("text")
    .attr("x", (plot.left + plot.right) / 2).attr("y", 397)
    .attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 13)
    .attr("fill", "currentColor").text("Time (half-lives)");

  svg.append("text")
    .attr("transform", `translate(365,${(plot.top + plot.bottom) / 2}) rotate(-90)`)
    .attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 13)
    .attr("fill", "currentColor").text("Nuclei remaining");

  const theoretical = d3.range(0, 5.001, 0.05).map(t => ({
    time: t,
    remaining: 100 * 2 ** (-t)
  }));
  const line = d3.line().x(d => x(d.time)).y(d => y(d.remaining));

  svg.append("path")
    .datum(theoretical)
    .attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#73777b")
    .attr("stroke-width", 2.5).attr("stroke-dasharray", "7,5")
    .attr("d", line);

  svg.append("path")
    .datum(observed)
    .attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "var(--d3-decay-accent, #7c3aed)")
    .attr("stroke-width", 3)
    .attr("d", line.curve(d3.curveStepAfter));

  const marker = svg.append("line")
    .attr("y1", plot.top).attr("y2", plot.bottom)
    .attr("stroke", "#d65f4a").attr("stroke-width", 2);

  const observedDot = svg.append("circle")
    .attr("r", 5.5).attr("fill", "#d65f4a")
    .attr("stroke", "var(--bs-body-bg, white)").attr("stroke-width", 2);

  const valueLabel = svg.append("text")
    .attr("x", plot.right).attr("y", 68)
    .attr("text-anchor", "end").attr("font-size", 13)
    .attr("fill", "currentColor");

  const legend = svg.append("g")
    .attr("transform", `translate(${plot.left + 12},${plot.bottom + 28})`)
    .attr("font-size", 12).attr("fill", "currentColor");
  legend.append("line").attr("x2", 25)
    .attr("stroke", "var(--d3-decay-accent, #7c3aed)").attr("stroke-width", 3);
  legend.append("text").attr("x", 32).attr("y", 4).text("Observed sample");
  legend.append("line").attr("x1", 145).attr("x2", 170)
    .attr("stroke", "#73777b").attr("stroke-width", 2.5)
    .attr("stroke-dasharray", "7,5");
  legend.append("text").attr("x", 177).attr("y", 4).text("Theoretical trend");

  return {node: svg.node(), description, circles, countLabel, marker,
    observedDot, valueLabel, x, y, reducedMotion};
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
decayFigure = {
  const remaining = nuclei.filter(d => d.decayTime > time).length;
  const expected = 100 * 2 ** (-time);
  const duration = chartState.reducedMotion ? 0 : 220;

  chartState.circles.interrupt().transition().duration(duration)
    .attr("r", d => d.decayTime > time ? 9 : 5)
    .attr("fill", d => d.decayTime > time ? "var(--d3-decay-accent, #7c3aed)" : "#adb5bd")
    .attr("stroke", d => d.decayTime > time ? "var(--d3-decay-accent-dark, #5b21b6)" : "#6c757d")
    .attr("opacity", d => d.decayTime > time ? 1 : 0.28);

  chartState.countLabel.text(`${remaining} of 100 remain`);
  chartState.marker.attr("x1", chartState.x(time)).attr("x2", chartState.x(time));
  chartState.observedDot
    .attr("cx", chartState.x(time)).attr("cy", chartState.y(remaining));
  chartState.valueLabel.text(`Observed ${remaining} · expected ${expected.toFixed(1)}`);
  chartState.description.text(
    `At ${time.toFixed(1)} half-lives, ${remaining} of 100 nuclei remain; ` +
    `the theoretical expectation is ${expected.toFixed(1)}.`
  );
  return chartState.node;
}
```

:::

The fading circles and the step-shaped line are not independent illustrations.
They are two views of the same array of 100 objects, so selecting a new time or
sample keeps every part of the explanation consistent.

## The reusable pattern

Quarto provides the reactive layer through Observable JS. The input values
`time` and `sample` become ordinary variables, and cells that use them are
automatically recalculated. D3 provides the lower-level control over the SVG.

First, load D3 and create a control:

````markdown
```{ojs}
d3 = require("d3@7")

viewof time = Inputs.range([0, 5], {
  value: 0,
  step: 0.1,
  label: "Time (half-lives)"
})
```
````

Each nucleus is represented by one object. Its position is fixed, while its
randomly generated `decayTime` determines its state at any selected time:

````markdown
```{ojs}
nuclei = {
  const random = seededRandom(2027);
  return d3.range(100).map(id => ({
    id,
    row: Math.floor(id / 10),
    column: id % 10,
    decayTime: -Math.log2(1 - random())
  }));
}
```
````

D3's data join creates one SVG circle per object. The `id` key keeps the link
between an object and its circle explicit:

```javascript
const circles = svg.append("g")
  .selectAll("circle")
  .data(nuclei, d => d.id)
  .join("circle")
  .attr("cx", d => grid.x + d.column * grid.spacing)
  .attr("cy", d => grid.y + d.row * grid.spacing)
  .attr("r", 9);
```

When `time` changes, the SVG is retained and its existing circles are updated.
Interrupting an unfinished transition makes rapid slider movement behave cleanly:

```javascript
circles
  .interrupt()
  .transition()
  .duration(220)
  .attr("r", d => d.decayTime > time ? 9 : 5)
  .attr("opacity", d => d.decayTime > time ? 1 : 0.28);
```

This separation is useful in larger examples: create the SVG structure once,
then write a small update step that maps the current reactive state onto it.

## Why use D3 here?

For a conventional scatter plot or bar chart, a higher-level tool such as
Observable Plot will usually require less code. D3 becomes attractive when the
teaching idea calls for custom visual marks, transitions, direct manipulation,
or several views that must update together.

The same pattern could be adapted without changing its overall architecture:

- nuclei could become cells surviving a treatment;
- discrete states could show molecules binding or changing conformation;
- a grid and summary could reveal repeated samples from a distribution;
- individuals could move between states in a population model; or
- marks could represent items moving through the steps of an algorithm.

The strongest use of interactivity is not simply to make a figure move. It is to
let learners change something meaningful and immediately see the consequences
in representations that support the intended explanation.
